t: Faulty Sensor — Detect Which Sensor Dropped a Data Point
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Both sensors recorded n samples, but at most one of them dropped exactly one sample: its remaining values shifted left one slot and its last slot got filled with some random value different from the dropped datum. We must name the defective sensor (1 or 2) or return -1 when neither is defective or the evidence is inconclusive. In Example 1 sensor2 = [2,1,3,4] looks like pristine data while sensor1 = [2,3,4,5] matches it with the value 1 dropped and a trailing 5 substituted — so sensor 1 is faulty. In Example 2 both readings are identical, so nothing is wrong: -1. With n <= 100 even testing every hypothetical drop position is cheap, and a linear suffix comparison also exists.
k: A faulty reading equals the true sequence with ONE element deleted (everything after shifts left) plus an arbitrary final value.
Everything before the first differing index is untouched by any deletion there or later, so only the suffix from that point needs checking.
Zero or two consistent hypotheses both mean indeterminate — they collapse to -1.

a.i: For each sensor in turn assume it is defective and the other holds true data. Try deleting each position d of the suspect array and verify against the truth: the first d values agree, values d through n-2 equal truth positions d+1 through n-1, and the final value differs from the dropped datum (the random filler never repeats it). Exactly one consistent sensor identifies the culprit; zero or two consistency verdicts mean -1.
s: Define consistent(suspect, truth): exists d such that suspect[:d] = truth[:d], suspect[d:n-1] = truth[d+1:n], and suspect[n-1] != truth[d].
Evaluate it for (sensor1, sensor2) and for (sensor2, sensor1).
Return 1 or 2 when exactly one holds.
Return -1 when both or neither hold.
a.t: O(n^2) — n candidate drop positions per hypothesis, each verified in O(n); trivial at n <= 100

a.n: Approach 2: Compare Shifted Suffixes from the First Mismatch
a.i: Locate the first index i where the arrays disagree; prefixes before i are identical and unaffected by any deletion at or after i. If sensor1 dropped its i-th value, its tail must satisfy sensor1[t] == sensor2[t+1] for every t from i to n-2 (its last entry is random). Symmetrically for sensor2. Exactly one satisfied check names the culprit; both or neither mean -1. When the sole difference sits at the final index, both checks hold vacuously yet either sensor could have dropped its last value — correctly reported as indeterminate.
s: Check A: sensor1[t] == sensor2[t+1] for all t in [i, n-2]; build check B symmetrically.
Return 1 if only A holds, 2 if only B holds.
a.t: O(n) — one scan for the mismatch plus one pass over the suffix

w:
**Wrap-up**

State the deletion model clearly, then go straight to the O(n) suffix comparison. Pitfalls: comparing fully shifted arrays from index 0 instead of starting at the first mismatch (positions before the mismatch need not match their shifted partners, e.g. [1,3,4,99] vs [1,2,3,4]); forgetting that the last element is random and unconstrained except for not repeating the dropped value; and treating identical arrays as a defect — that is -1 too. Follow-up: if several data points could drop, alignment becomes longest-common-subsequence style matching between the two readings.
